content: The expiration of a manufacturer's patent led to a reduction in the period of profitable market exclusivity for pioneer drug manufacturers. Simultaneously, new regulations were interpreted to mandate comprehensive safety and efficacy testing for generic versions of approved drugs. Court rulings obtained by pioneer manufacturers prohibited generic manufacturers from initiating clinical trials while the original drug remained under patent protection. The Hatch-Waxman Act was designed as a compromise between pioneer and generic drug manufacturers. Its goal was to lower the overall cost of bringing generic drugs to market, thereby reducing long-term drug prices, while maintaining the profitability of developing new drugs. The Act extended the patent exclusivity period for new drugs, linking these extensions partially to the duration of the FDA approval process for each drug. For generic manufacturers, the Act introduced the Abbreviated New Drug Application (ANDA) process, which required them to demonstrate that their generic formulation had the same active ingredient, route of administration, dosage form, strength, and pharmacokinetic properties (bioequivalence) as the corresponding brand-name drug. This legislation is credited with establishing the modern generic drug industry. During the AIDS epidemic, concerns about the length of the drug approval process became prominent. In the mid-to-late 1980s, HIV activist groups like ACT-UP accused the FDA of unnecessarily delaying the approval of medications for HIV and opportunistic infections. Protests, such as the October 11, 1988 demonstration at the FDA campus, highlighted these frustrations, resulting in nearly 180 arrests. In 1990, Dr. Louis Lasagna, chair of a presidential advisory panel on drug approval, estimated that thousands of lives were lost annually due to delays in the approval and marketing of drugs for cancer and AIDS. In response to these criticisms, the FDA implemented new rules to expedite the approval of drugs for life-threatening diseases and expanded pre-approval access to drugs for patients with limited treatment options. One of the first new rules was the IND exemption or treatment IND rule, which allowed expanded access to drugs undergoing Phase II or III trials (or, in extraordinary cases, even earlier) if the drug potentially offered a safer or better alternative to existing treatments for terminal or serious illnesses. Another rule, the parallel track policy, enabled drug companies to establish mechanisms for patients who could not participate in clinical trials to access potentially life-saving drugs. The parallel track designation could be made at the time of IND submission. These accelerated approval rules were further expanded and codified in 1992. All initial drugs approved for HIV/AIDS treatment utilized these mechanisms. For example, a treatment IND was issued for the first HIV drug, AZT, in 1985, and it was approved just two years later in 1987. Three of the first five drugs targeting HIV were approved in the United States before being approved in any other country. An ongoing court case, Abigail Alliance v. von Eschenbach, has the potential to significantly alter FDA regulations regarding unapproved drugs. Abigail Burroughs, a college student diagnosed with head and neck cancer, sought access to the experimental drug cetuximab, which was only available in clinical trials for colon cancer at the time. Her father sued the FDA, arguing that terminal cancer patients have a Constitutionally protected right to access experimental medications before FDA approval. The Abigail Alliance contended that the FDA should license drugs for terminally ill patients with desperate diagnoses after Phase I testing. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia initially ruled in favor of the Abigail Alliance, recognizing the right of terminally ill patients to access unapproved treatments. However, the case was scheduled for rehearing at the FDA's request. This case could profoundly impact clinical cancer research, as the initial ruling effectively allows unrestricted access to experimental drugs for terminally ill patients, potentially reducing incentives for participation in Phase II and III clinical trials. The recall of Vioxx, a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) linked to fatal heart attacks in thousands of Americans, catalyzed a wave of safety reforms at the FDA. Approved in 1999, Vioxx was initially believed to be safer than previous NSAIDs due to its reduced risk of gastrointestinal bleeding. However, preand post-marketing studies suggested an increased risk of myocardial infarction, which was conclusively demonstrated in the APPROVe trial in 2004. Facing numerous lawsuits, the manufacturer voluntarily withdrew Vioxx from the market. The Vioxx case has fueled ongoing debates about whether new drugs should be evaluated based on their absolute safety or their safety relative to existing treatments for the same condition. In the aftermath of the recall, there were widespread calls for reforms in the FDA's preand post-market drug safety regulations from major newspapers, medical journals, consumer advocacy groups, lawmakers, and FDA officials. A committee of 16 experts, including leaders in clinical medicine, medical research, economics, biostatistics, law, public policy, public health, and allied health professions, as well as current and former executives from the pharmaceutical, hospital, and health insurance industries, identified significant deficiencies in the FDA's current system for ensuring the safety of drugs on the American market.
